newsitem.title: INDIA: Rescue teams clear rubble after deadly India quake.
newsitem.headline: Rescue teams clear rubble after deadly India quake.

text.p: Rescue teams searched on Friday for survivors in the debris left by a powerful earthquake that killed dozens of people in central India, injured more than 1,000 and left at least as many homeless.

Troops, volunteers and government rescue teams used pick-axes and shovels to clear the rubble after the quake, measuring 6.0 on the Richter scale, swept through the state of Madhya Pradesh before dawn on Thursday.
At least 38 people were killed when the tremor struck, flattening houses and burying many victims as they slept, officials said.
Many panic-stricken residents of the city of Jabalpur shifted their beds outdoors, saying they feared possible aftershocks.
"I've not taken my family inside the house, and I do not plan to either," said Jabalapur resident Sunderlal Tiwari. He said five people in the house next to his had been buried in their sleep.
Local government officials tried to coax people to return to their homes. "It won't occur again," Ajay Singh, a senior official, repeatedly told people.
Singh said the government had set up nine relief camps that could house 100 people each as a temporary relief measure.
Officials said they did not expect the death toll to rise significantly.
Authorities said about 200 people were in serious condition in hospital. Most sustained head and spinal injuries or broken bones.

The earthquake was centred on the village of Kosamghat, 23 km (14 miles) south of Jabalpur. All the village's 160 houses, mostly mud huts, were flattened, leaving more than 1,000 residents homeless, elder Mohan Lal Yadav said.

Forty villagers were injured but no one was killed because people were sleeping outside in the early summer heat. "Had this been a winter night, not a single person would have survived," said 65-year-old Shanti Bal.
In nearby Donda Mehgaon village, four people were killed and numerous water buffaloes, used to produce milk or work in the wheat fields, were crushed in their sheds, residents said.
In September 1993, about 10,000 people were killed in neighbouring Maharashtra state when an earthquake measuring 6.3 on the Richter scale struck the Latur-Osmanabad region.

A seismology department official in New Delhi said the quake in Latur was much closer to the surface than the one in Madhya Pradesh, making it more deadly. In addition, the soil in central India was more solid.
The quake was felt across a wide swathe of northern, central and eastern India and woke up people in the capital New Delhi, 720 km (450 miles) to the northwest.
